passage: Bidisha's tea stall near the Bankura bus stand had lost half its customers since spring. "It's the new bakery opposite," she told Lakshmi, who sold flowers beside her. "And the heat. And this year's bad luck, what to do." Lakshmi nodded, but she had seen other things. Bidisha opened at nine now, not seven, and the morning bus crowd had found somewhere else. She had snapped at a regular for asking for less sugar. The cups were chipped. "Maybe open early again?" Lakshmi tried. Bidisha waved it away. "The problem isn't me, didi. Everything is against me this year." She said it almost proudly, like someone refusing to be blamed. By evening she had sold eleven cups.

qa.a: At nine, not seven.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Bidisha's falling sales?

passage: In the small meeting room at the phone showroom, Farhan's quarterly review was not going well. "Sales are down again," said Ganga, the branch manager, sliding the sheet across. passage: The rain had flooded the underpass, and Arohi reached the interview in Andheri twenty minutes late, her shoes soaked. That part really was bad luck. For a second she thought of the empty notes page on her laptop. Then she closed her eyes and thought instead of the panel's bored faces.

I've had four jobs in three years, and I'll tell you why none of them worked. I'm Alka.
The first boss was jealous of me. The second company was a mess; they didn't know how to use talent. The third, the market crashed, it wasn't my fault. The fourth, well, the manager just had favourites.
My friend Ojas listens to all this. Last week he asked, “In all four, was there anything you'd do differently?”
I said no. Honestly, I couldn't think of anything. It's been bad luck and bad people. What was I supposed to do?
He didn't argue. He just said, “Four is a lot of bad luck.”
I laughed. But on the drive home, it annoyed me. I think it annoyed me because I didn't have an answer.

Team supervisor's note, sales, quarterly review.
Neelam has missed her target for the third quarter running. In our meeting she listed reasons: the market is slow, the leads she gets are bad, head office favours the Mumbai team, and the new product is “impossible to sell.”
All of these may be partly true. But her colleague Zeenat, working with the same leads and product, met her target. When I mentioned this, Neelam said Zeenat “always gets lucky.”
I asked Neelam what she would change about her own approach. She looked surprised, then irritated, and said there was nothing, it was all outside her control.
I think she is protecting her pride. Admitting her own part would feel like failing.
Next steps: I have asked Zeenat, with Neelam's agreement, to let Neelam shadow two of her client calls, and we will meet to discuss one thing within Neelam's control for next quarter.

qa.q: How many quarters in a row has Neelam missed her target?
qa.a: She has missed it three quarters running.

qa.q: Why might Neelam react with irritation when asked about her own approach?
qa.a: She seems to be protecting her pride; admitting her part would feel like failing.

qa.q: What did the supervisor arrange, and why could it help?
qa.a: Shadowing two of Zeenat's calls and then naming one thing within Neelam's control, so she can learn instead of only blaming.

Wednesday.
Another rejection for the café loan. Of course. The bank officer clearly didn't like me. Banks never lend to people like us. And the market for cafés is saturated anyway.
Shreya came over with chai and read the rejection letter. She said, “It says the business plan didn't show the monthly costs.”
I said that was an excuse. They'd have found something else.
She said, “Maybe. But what if the costs part is real?”
I got annoyed and changed the subject. It's always the same: the bank, the landlord, the economy. Nothing I do seems to matter.
But after she left, I looked at my business plan. There was no monthly costs page. I'd skipped it because I hate spreadsheets.
I don't want to think about it tonight.
— Nazia

Hansa's tailoring shop in Ujjain had lost half its customers in a year. Every evening she explained it to her brother Saurabh the same way. "It's that new mall. People want ready-made now. And my luck, what to say. Everything is against me."
Saurabh, sorting buttons, said carefully, "Mrs Joshi said her blouse came four days late. And the Sharma girls said the fitting was loose twice."
"Mrs Joshi changed the design at the last minute," Hansa snapped. "And the Sharma girls never came for the trial. Not my fault."
"Maybe we could note the delivery dates?"
"What for? The mall doesn't care about my dates."
She threw a piece of cloth on the counter. Saurabh didn't bring it up again. Outside, a customer peeked in, saw the pile of unfinished orders on the table, and walked on.

Pablo had lost his third kitchen job in Madrid in a year. He told his friend Tomas about it over beers in the plaza.
"The chef hated me from day one. Like the last one. Honestly, these places are all the same. They want robots."
Tomas turned his glass. "What did he say when he let you go?"
"Something about being late. Like that's a crime in a kitchen."
"Were you late?"
"A few times. The metro is a disaster in the mornings, you know that."
"The last place said the same thing."
Pablo waved his hand. "Bad luck. Bad bosses. Bad city, maybe." He laughed, but his jaw was tight. "Anyway. I'll find a better kitchen."
Tomas didn't answer. He'd heard "a better kitchen" twice before.

qa.a: He said something about Pablo being late.
